entry.title: An outside reverse-engineering toolkit evaluated from its documentation: not adopted, one idea taken
entry.summary: The owner asked whether REA, an open-source toolkit that gives AI agents reverse-engineering tools over the Model Context Protocol, could speed this project up. A research agent read its documentation; nothing was installed or run. The answer is that the product does not fit this project as it stands, and that its central idea is worth building here from what the project already has.
entry.content:
The owner asked whether REA, an open-source toolkit that gives AI agents reverse-engineering tools over the Model Context Protocol, could speed this project up. A research agent read its documentation; nothing was installed or run. The answer is that the product does not fit this project as it stands, and that its central idea is worth building here from what the project already has.

What was asked

Where do lanes lose time that a shared tool could save? Every lane that names a function or maps a large one first writes its own throwaway script to collect the same evidence: the strings a function references, its callers and callees, the class whose virtual table points at it, the names of its neighbours. A naming lane spends 10 to 30 minutes on that before it names anything, and sixty lanes do it at once.

What was found

QuestionWhat the documentation saysStatus
Can it use the project's analysed disassembler project?No. Each session imports a private copy of the binary into a temporary project and analyses it again; it never opens an existing project.Verified from its installation and provider pages.
Does it work on this machine?Its Windows support is described as experimental, read-only and for x64 hosts. This machine is an ARM64 host running x64 tools under emulation, which the documentation does not mention.Verified for what it says; unknown for this machine.
Can many lanes share it?Not stated. Each connection starts its own analysis engine with a default heap of 2 GB.Inferred: sixty lanes would each pay an import and a virtual machine.
Can it dump evidence for many functions in one run?No batch command is documented. Batch decompilation exists as an agent tool inside one session; a session's evidence can be exported once and read later without the engine.Verified for what is documented; three reference pages could not be read.
Does it help name functions that reference no strings?No similar-function search, no library signature matching, and no virtual-table or type-information recovery for Windows programs are documented.Verified as absent from the pages read.
Does its showcase's verification apply here?The showcase that runs thousands of cases against original code uses a harness written by the case study's author, not part of the toolkit.Verified. This project's checker already does more.
Stability and set-upFive releases with breaking changes in one week; set-up edits agent configuration for the user account, not per project.Verified.

What was decided

  • Not adopted. Nothing was installed.
  • The idea taken: one shared, queryable source of evidence for every lane. A tool lane is building one database for all game functions from the mapped image (calls, data references, strings, virtual tables, names, neighbours, and a simple signature for finding instances of one routine), with a script that prints a compact dossier per function. It holds no disassembly and no decompiler output and stays in the build area. Once proven on a real naming list it goes into the naming, production and large-function briefs.
  • For the owner to decide: the project's own disassembler could export pseudocode and basic-block listings for every function in one unattended run, kept out of the repository as all decompiler output is. That is several hours of processor time and has not been started.

What was confusing

An export of the call graph and cross-references made on 3 October was on disk all along (30,900 functions, 79,000 call pairs, 151,000 references) and no brief pointed lanes at it. It is older than the inventory and misses about 6,500 functions, so the new database is built from the image and checked against it.

entry.title: Three questions about the checker settled in a day, and an audit that withdrew two verified rewrites
entry.summary: Three things that lanes reported about the checker on 11 October were each given to an investigation lane before anyone acted on them. Two came back settled inside twenty minutes of work. The third, an audit of how verified rewrites convert floats to integers, found a real fault: two verified rewrites were withdrawn the same afternoon, and 288 more functions are being tested.
entry.content:
Three things that lanes reported about the checker on 11 October were each given to an investigation lane before anyone acted on them. Two came back settled inside twenty minutes of work. The third, an audit of how verified rewrites convert floats to integers, found a real fault: two verified rewrites were withdrawn the same afternoon, and 288 more functions are being tested.

A scripted callee's writes are the same on every call within a trial

What was asked: two lanes on two large functions (a file parser that reads a token per line, and a search loop that calls one callee per candidate) stopped on the belief that a scripted callee cannot write different words through its pointer argument on each call within a trial. Is that so?

FactStatusWhat it means
A callee's return value can follow a sequence that advances with each call inside a trial.Verified on the stock checker: a three-step sequence passes 200 of 200 where a once-per-trial answer fails 200 of 200.Use the per-call form for a callee that is called several times; use the per-trial form for one that is called once (an earlier entry records the opposite mistake).
The words a callee writes through a pointer are one row per trial.Verified from the worker's source and by experiment: each call writes the same words at its own destination. They do not depend on the call's index, on an argument, or on the call site for one stub.The two lanes were right about the limit.
What a lane can do today, with no change.Verified in a private copy, inferred for the stock build: a callee that returns a pointer can be given a sequence of pointers to different words, so its caller reads a different answer per call. Calls at different sites can have a stub each. A handler can be proven in a stage of its own with the token fixed for the trial.A stage with the token fixed proves that handler's code. It does not prove the transitions between handlers within one run, their order, or that one handler's exit state is valid for the next: those are listed as not covered.
A candidate extension: a per-call list of write rows.Built in a private copy only. Its regression contract fails to load on the stock driver and passes on the private build with a wrong version caught; the checker's own set gives identical verdicts on both builds for 61 of 62 contracts, the other being the absolute-read self-test that cannot run on this machine.Not adopted. It changes the worker and the driver, so it needs a checker review lane and a new checker version before any proof may use it.

The same lane found that the manual's line on scripted writes gives the count in the wrong unit: the count is in 32-bit words and the destination offset in bytes. An earlier lane lost an hour to exactly that.

The option for unrelocated absolute reads

Settled the same morning and recorded in its own entry: the option cannot set up on this machine. A follow-up worth recording here: the lane whose route seemed to need it ran the relocation checker on its function and found all 52 absolute operands relocated. The fault on that route has another cause, as every earlier claim of this kind had.

Float-to-integer conversions written with Rust's cast

What was asked: a lift lane noticed that two verified rewrites convert a float to an integer differently when the value is not a number or does not fit. The original's instruction gives a fixed result there; Rust's cast gives zero or the nearest end of the range. How many verified rewrites use the cast where the original's instruction behaves differently, and do their proofs cover those inputs?

FactValueStatus
Float-to-integer casts found326 certain, in 291 of 15,700 verified rewrites; 465 more that the detector could not type, not counted.Verified: a hand check of 30 flagged and 30 unflagged files found no false alarm and no miss on the final pass.
A random sample of 4028 are guarded in the rewrite so that it gives the processor's value; 5 agree on the bits that are used; 7 have no guard, in three functions.Verified for the 33; the 7 are unsettled.
The sevenThe lane's pairing of each cast with the original's instruction was unreliable, and a checker run on one of the three functions, whose contract should draw floats that overflow the cast, still passed 300 trials.Unknown: either the rewrite is wrong and the proof cannot see it, or the classification is wrong.
Estimate if the seven are realAbout 51 verified rewrites (25 to 93); about 7 if they are not.Inferred from the sample.

What was decided at first: nothing is withdrawn on an estimate. A second lane settled the three functions one by one: the original's conversion identified exactly by following the data, both sides computed on the special values, and any difference shown on the stock checker with a contract widened to reach them.

Settled the same afternoon

FunctionWhat the original doesResult on the stock checker
An audio query routine: six values converted and stored as 16-bit wordsA 32-bit truncating conversion, of which 16 bits are kept. For a positive value too large for 32 bits the original stores zero; the rewrite's cast stored the largest 16-bit value.Verified. The contract of record passes because its floats are small. With only two inputs steered out of range, the tracked rewrite fails 439 of 1,000 trials; a corrected conversion passes 1,000 of 1,000 with the old form failing as the wrong version. Withdrawn.
A small task routine: one value converted through a 64-bit integer storeAn x87 store of a 64-bit integer under truncation, of which the low half is used. The two sides differ only for positive infinity and values too large for 64 bits.Verified. With a global the game fills at run time steered that high, the tracked rewrite fails 67 of 1,000; the corrected form passes. Withdrawn. Whether the game can produce such a value there is unknown.
A fill routine with five conversionsFive 32-bit truncating conversions whose operands the code itself bounds: a counter that never exceeds 64.Verified safe. An instrumented run logged 24,984 operands, all in range. Not withdrawn.

The first lane's puzzle is explained: the proof that passed with inputs that "should overflow" never drew such inputs; its float cycles were small. That is the general lesson. A contract's ordinary float ranges do not reach the values on which a cast and an instruction differ, so a proof with ordinary ranges says nothing about them.

What was decided

  • The two rewrites are withdrawn; the verified count went down by two, with the reason in the changelog. A strengthening lane is proving the corrected copies with the contract of record and the widened contract together.
  • Production, queue and large-function briefs now carry the rule: a float is never converted with a bare cast unless the code bounds it first; otherwise the conversion is written to match the instruction, and the function's contract must reach not-a-number, the infinities and values past each end of the range, with a wrong version that uses the bare cast.
  • A scripted version of the widened test is being built and run over the other 288 functions that have such a cast. A pass counts only if the special values are shown to have reached the cast. The verified count may go down again.

How to reproduce

The two audit lanes' folders hold the detector for such casts, the list of 326, the classified sample, the widened contracts, the corrected rewrites, and the two conversion functions with their bit-level references and tests.

entry.title: Six operating faults of one night, five of them in the coordinator's own tooling
entry.summary: This entry records what went wrong in running the lanes between the evening of 10 October and the afternoon of 11 October, so that the next coordinator does not find each of them again. None of them produced a false result. Together they cost about nine hours of machine time.
entry.content:
This entry records what went wrong in running the lanes between the evening of 10 October and the afternoon of 11 October, so that the next coordinator does not find each of them again. None of them produced a false result. Together they cost about nine hours of machine time.

What happenedCauseWhat was changed
The machine went into standby from 07:06 to 11:33 and from 13:06 to 15:16. Nothing was verified for eight hours. Four Haiku lanes failed for want of a network and every background window ended at once.Verified from the system's power events. The request that keeps the machine awake is held by the coordinator's session and lapses when the session has been idle for five minutes. One interrupted turn of the coordinator was enough.The request was renewed and everything restarted; the lanes of the other model survived the standby and resumed by themselves. A hold on sleep that does not depend on the coordinator's session is the owner's decision and has been put to him.
Naming stood still for five hours with 1,300 functions unnamed and no naming lane running.Verified. The second naming pass left alone any function handed out in the last twelve hours, in case its lane was still running. After a burst of 35 naming lanes that covered nearly all of what was left, so the pass saw nothing to do. Naming had also been left out of the rotation of lane kinds.The pass asks the lane's log whether it is still running. Naming is in the rotation. The final pass uses small batches and tells each lane to read every function in full, since a survey of strings and neighbours had already failed on them.
The coordinator's re-run of a finished lane's proofs broke without cause, several times in the night, and one lane's twice in a row.Verified. The watchdog that stops processes left behind by ended lanes matched the re-run itself, because the re-run names the ended lane's contract. A broken re-run imports nothing and holds nothing, so nothing false was recorded.The watchdog skips any process whose command line names the coordinator's own folder.
Regression lanes were about to be told there was nothing left to re-run.Verified. See the entry on the regression runner: proofs handed to a lane and never reached counted as taken for good.What an ended lane did not reach is handed out again.
With sixty and more lanes, output fell to half of what thirty produced, and the coordinator's own commands took ten minutes.Measured over four hours: about 19,000 bytes of newly verified code an hour at about sixty lanes against 25,000 to 51,000 at thirty. The machine has 18 logical processors; memory was never the limit.Lanes of the other model and the regression runner run below normal priority; two finishers work the list of ended lanes from both ends, each lane claimed before it is worked on. The lane count itself is the owner's decision: he has chosen to fill memory, and each hour's figure is reported so the effect can be seen.
A lane left a search running over every lane folder for eighty minutes; another lane's command reached 3.2 GB.Verified. A recursive search of the whole scratch tree (2,500 folders) started by a lane and abandoned when its command timed out.The first was stopped by hand, by process id; the second by the guard that stops a project process above 3 GB. Lane prompts for investigation lanes now say never to search the whole scratch tree.

Signs worth knowing

  • A Haiku lane can hang with nothing running and no notice. The sign: no log line for fifteen minutes, no process whose command line names the lane, and no new file in its folder. Stop it and resume it with its context; if it hangs again, start a fresh session in the same folder with a short finishing prompt.
  • A lane of the other model that writes nothing to its lane log for half an hour is usually working: its own session log is the thing to look at.
  • After a standby, runs that were in progress are void: the drivers' time limits expire and the re-run records a timeout, which holds the claim until it is cleared and repeated.

entry.title: Old proofs are now re-run by a script, and the list of what was left had been wrong
entry.summary: About 13,700 functions are recorded as verified on an earlier version of the checker. Re-running each proof of record unchanged on the current checker, with its wrong version, is the regression the plan calls for. Until this morning lanes did it, slowly. A tool lane turned it into a script in 43 minutes, and wiring the script in showed that the process had been about to run out of work it could see.
entry.content:
About 13,700 functions are recorded as verified on an earlier version of the checker. Re-running each proof of record unchanged on the current checker, with its wrong version, is the regression the plan calls for. Until this morning lanes did it, slowly. A tool lane turned it into a script in 43 minutes, and wiring the script in showed that the process had been about to run out of work it could see.

What was asked

Six regression lanes settled 27 to 95 proofs each of the 350 each was given, in a hundred minutes: about 80 an hour for the project, a week for the backlog. Each lane wrote its own preparation, build and run scripts before running anything. Can the mechanical part be one resumable tool that needs no model?

What was found

FactValueWhat it means
The runner on its 123 test functions123 hold, every wrong version rejected, about 13 seconds a function with three workers. Stopped by process id in mid-run and restarted, it skipped what was settled and repeated nothing.Verified. The tool builds tracked rewrites in crates of thirty (a crate that fails is split in half, so one bad file costs only itself), runs each contract of record on the stock driver in a process of its own with a time limit, then the saved wrong version at 100 trials.
Its first full list: 350 proofs first recorded on checker version 5311 hold; 33 pass but have no saved wrong version; 5 could not run; 1 fails.Verified. The 311 are recorded on the current checker. The one that fails goes to the queue of old proofs that do not hold.
Proofs first recorded on checker versions 1 to 45,395 functions. Of 350 tried: 83 pass unchanged, with no wrong version to run; 2 hold.Verified. A wrong version per function was not required until version 5. These need one written, which is a lane's work; the runner can do the build and the thousand trials first.
The list maker for regression lanesIt reported 1,636 proofs left to hand out. 13,700 were still to re-run.Verified. It counted every proof ever handed to a regression lane as taken for good, and lanes reached a quarter of what they were given. After the correction it sees 6,857: what an ended lane did not reach is handed out again.

Three faults in the tool, found on real lists and corrected

  • Rewrites of the first weeks name the runtime's macros without a path, because their proving crates imported them at the crate root. The tool's crates did not, and 257 of 350 early rewrites failed to build for that one reason.
  • Some lanes' tracked rewrites carry their wrong version in the same file. The tool added the lane's saved copy as well, the name was defined twice, the build failed, and the tool dropped the wrong version and reported that none was saved: 19 of the first 30 proofs of one list.
  • The tool recorded what it could not settle as deferred. Its first list would have put 348 verified functions into the deferral queues as if they had failed. Such rows are now written as not reached, with the reason; the rows of that first list were corrected before anything imported them.

What was decided

  • The runner works through the proofs recorded on versions 5 to 7 (5,599 functions) in lists of 150, one list after another, below normal priority; the coordinator's import records each hold.
  • Regression lanes take the proofs without a wrong version, oldest first.
  • Nine proofs that a lane had recorded as unable to run (its worker was lost on them) hold under the runner; they are not counted until they have run once more.

What went wrong

In its first hour the runner ran at normal priority beside thirty production lanes that run below normal, and the hour's newly verified code halved. A re-run of old proofs must not take the processor from new work.

How to reproduce

The runner, its wrapper and the loop that makes lists and imports them are in the coordinator's scratch folder; the tool lane's folder has the agreement table against two regression lanes and the stop-and-resume test.

entry.title: Eight large functions closed in one night, and what each close taught about proofs
entry.summary: Between the evening of 10 October and the afternoon of 11 October, Claude Haiku 5.5 lanes closed eight functions of 2,200 to 4,500 bytes that lanes of the other model had left partly proven in stages: 26,000 bytes of code in all. None closed in one session; they took one to five sessions each. The coordinator re-ran every one before importing it. Five of the eight were sent back at least once after being reported as verified, and the reasons for sending them back are the useful part of this entry.
entry.content:
Between the evening of 10 October and the afternoon of 11 October, Claude Haiku 5.5 lanes closed eight functions of 2,200 to 4,500 bytes that lanes of the other model had left partly proven in stages: 26,000 bytes of code in all. None closed in one session; they took one to five sessions each. The coordinator re-ran every one before importing it. Five of the eight were sent back at least once after being reported as verified, and the reasons for sending them back are the useful part of this entry.

What was asked

The owner's rule of 10 October: Haiku lanes take the higher difficulties when the other model is struggling. The question for the night was whether a function left in stages can be closed at all, and what a lane must be told to do it.

What was found

FindingStatusWhat it means for the next lane
A wrong version that passes is a fault in the contract, not a limitation to list.Verified. A lane reported a function verified while listing that a version with one subtraction reversed still passed. Sent back to find out why, it found in six minutes that its 47 contracts placed a table of floats at the wrong address (the image address had not been turned into an offset from the image base), so the table read as zero on both sides and everything multiplied by it vanished.When a wrong version passes, find out why before anything else: a fixture at the wrong address, a value multiplied by a zero fill, cycles of equal length that pair two paths, a word that no check compares. Every lane's brief now says so.
A function with unwritten branches is not verified, however good the proof of the rest.Verified. One rewrite was reported verified with nine deliberate faults in it, seven marked as not written. Sent back, the lane showed by experiment that five of the seven are paths on which the original itself faults (it dereferences a null it was just handed), and wrote and proved the other two.Each deliberate fault left in a rewrite is classified: a path the original faults on or can never take, with the evidence, may stay and is listed; a path the original completes must be written and proven.
"Partly proven" can mean untested inputs, not unwritten code.Verified. A lane ended with a 4,490-byte function recorded as partly proven and a list of open items. A fresh session asked to classify them found that none was unwritten code: they were combinations of inputs passing through code already proven on other inputs, and two branches the original can never take. The function closed in 17 minutes.Before a function is left as partly proven, the question is asked of every open item: is it code that is not there, or inputs that were not run? Only the first keeps a function open; the second is listed as a narrowing.
The published rewrite must not carry its wrong versions.Verified. Two lanes kept their wrong versions as switches inside the function body (sixteen in one file). The file was folded to its correct arms, rebuilt, and re-proven before import; the wrong versions stay in a second build.One export, no wrong-version parameter, and the clean file is the one the clean build compiled, byte for byte.
An earlier stage can be wrong and still pass.Verified, several times: a callee modelled as writing nothing when it increments the count a later loop reads; a contract that pinned two values equal so that reading the wrong one could not show; a contract in which half the trials faulted identically on both sides and proved nothing; a probe that never reached a route because one scripted lookup always answered zero.Re-run the inherited stages on your own build first, then distrust them where your new stage disagrees. A trial that faults on both sides is not a pass: the original must complete.
The coordinator's re-run must read a proof in the form the lane kept it.Verified. One function was held by the re-run for a reason of form: its wrong versions were kept as 33 contracts of their own, each identical to a passing contract except for the library and the export, and the re-run read them as failing claims. The re-run now recognises such pairs by content and requires the wrong one to fail on a comparison.Either form is accepted: a wrong version declared in the contract, or a paired contract that differs only in library and export.

What worked as a way of briefing

  • An ordered list of small routes where the function is mapped; one narrow job where it is not (a frame map by experiment, one loop pass, one block built call by call against a probe that checks the first mismatch has moved); a checker investigation lane before anyone believes a reported checker fault.
  • Sending a lane back with the open items in order works: lanes stopped with most of their time unused in most first sessions, and continued when told what was left.
  • When a lane has grown long and stalls, a fresh session in the same lane folder with a short finishing prompt (reproduce the logged runs, replace the stale files, record the result) finished two functions in 10 and 17 minutes.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two functions took six and seven sessions and are still open, one with five routes left. The same belief about the checker stopped two lanes on two functions (see the entry on scripted writes). A lane session can hang with nothing running and no notice: the sign is no log line, no process of the lane's own and no new file for fifteen minutes.

How to reproduce

The briefing forms are in the coordinator's scratch folder as the per-lane additions to the queue brief; each closed function's lane folder holds its stage contracts, wrong versions and verdicts, and the coordinator's re-run of each is beside them.

entry.title: Lift: task block, turn, aim, flag, entry and record-scan routines (ped_task group, eight shapes)
entry.summary: From lane l-free18.
entry.content:
From lane l-free18.

Asked. Lift the 118 verified routines named as the ped task group that the earlier lane had not settled, grouped by the data they share rather than by name, one shape at a time, each lifted routine proven against its verified 32-bit rewrite.

Found (Verified). The names do not match the structures. Four names are shared by different routines: the aim update (four routines), the range check (two), the heading update (two) and the state initialiser (two). Grouping by what the rewrites read and write through their first argument gives eight shapes that could be lifted with a small owned type each, a set of forwarders with constant arguments, a set of routines whose target is computed from an index, and a set of routines that walk several objects. Nine routines in eight shapes were lifted; the rest is listed by reason in the lane's results.

ShapeRoutines liftedProofLeft out, and why
One task object: two read-only predicates24 differential tests; 9 wrong versions caughtIndex-computed pool accessors (3); a forwarder
Task state block reset12 differential tests; 5 wrong versions caughtNone in the shape
Task block constructor (seven callees)12 differential tests; 6 wrong versions caughtA 170-entry preset id table (decision needed)
Turn tracker (two trigonometric callees)12 differential tests; 10 wrong versions caughtDouble-precision callee (not callable from stable Rust)
Typed-record table scan12 differential tests; 7 wrong versions caughtA link-chain range check (two hops) and a global-row range check
Aim record update (two collaborators)12 differential tests; 7 wrong versions caughtOther aim updates (different objects)
Owner subject-flag update (six collaborators)12 differential tests; 6 wrong versions caughtNone in the shape
Entry initialiser (four collaborators)12 differential tests; 6 wrong versions caughtNone in the shape

Finding (Verified). Two verified rewrites in this group convert a float to an integer in different ways. The block constructor's rewrite uses the Rust conversion, which gives zero for a not-a-number and saturates outside the signed 32-bit range. The entry initialiser's rewrite gives the processor's truncating result, the most negative integer, for both. The lift of each follows its own rewrite. For the block constructor the difference cannot arise in the game: the two factors it reads from the image are one over 2^15 and minus 500, so the product stays between minus 500 and zero for any sixteen-bit draw. The proof of each shows the difference is measured, not assumed.

Finding (Verified). In the aim update, a not-a-number first direction component kept a different sign in the lift until the operand order of the single-precision operations was pinned with the same opaque-operand helper the rewrite uses. The rewrite was not changed.

Finding (Inferred). One routine copies a 170-entry preset table into the task system. The table is game data, so copying it into tracked source needs a decision; it is left out.

Decided. Each shape gets its own owned type, named for its data, in a separate module: none of the shapes shares a structure, so no single class was lifted. Collaborators travel as one trait per routine; their constant arguments are supplied by the implementation, and the proof compares the calls in order with their arguments. Callee-written scratch words are compared as non-null tokens; the proof does not compare their contents. Wrong versions each change one thing, and the proof prints how often each wrong version differs from its rewrite.

How to reproduce. Build the eight differential test programs of the test crate for the 32-bit target and run them one at a time; then run the host tests of the peds-tasks crate on the 64-bit host. The include paths in the test crate are local to the lane's scratch tree and are shortened by the integration script.

entry.title: Lift: task event table, task manager slots and the audio task record (ped_task group)
entry.summary: From lane l-free17.
entry.content:
From lane l-free17.

Asked. Lift the 149 verified routines named as the task family, grouped by the data they share rather than by name, one shape at a time, each lifted routine proven against its verified 32-bit rewrite.

Found (Verified). The name group is not one structure. Grouping by what the rewrites read and write through their first argument gives at least seven unrelated shapes, a family of forwarders with constant arguments, and receiver routines. Three shapes had clear data and were lifted, and one single owner-slot routine was lifted with them: a 32-record table of event and deadline records (9 routines), the task manager's pointer arrays and bomb requests (5 routines), and the audio task record (8 routines, three of them one generic release and two of them one generic stamp).

ShapeRoutines liftedProofLeft out, and why
Event table (owned table of records)918 differential tests; 17 wrong versions caughtA forwarder with one constant call; two receiver routines
Manager pointer arrays510 differential tests; 8 wrong versions caughtOne routine on an embedded sub-object
Audio task record813 differential tests; 12 wrong versions caughtA pointer walk; two indexed-table writes
Owner slot (one routine)12 differential tests; 2 wrong versions caughtNothing; the sibling receiver routines are listed in the lane report

Finding (Verified). One rewrite's comment says its return value is the address just past its table. The constant it returns lies 24 bytes beyond the end of the table. The lift follows the constant, and the lift does not return the value at all; no caller was checked.

Finding (Verified). The window routine's comments name two deadline words "first" and "second", and the stamp routines that write the same words name them the other way round. The lift names the words by what writes them and documents the window routine's reads.

Finding (Inferred). An indexed-table write routine, on the branch where its index byte is all ones, computes a zero base and writes at a small absolute address. This routine was not lifted. Whether that branch can be reached in the game is not established.

Decided. Helper addresses that a routine passes to a helper are rebuilt in the proof from the record index the lift passes. Each helper is a trait method; no operating-system call is in any lifted routine. Callee effects are assumed not to write the table or the record, and that assumption is listed in each routine's registry row.

How to reproduce. Build and run the four differential test programs of the test crate for the 32-bit target, then the host tests of the peds-tasks crate on the 64-bit host. The test crate's include paths are local to the lane's scratch tree.

entry.title: Ped task mover, seek record and task id lookup lifted and proven
entry.summary: From lane l-free16.
entry.content:
From lane l-free16.

Asked. Lift the group of verified free functions named as the peds-tasks part of the ped task family (109 routines, about 93 KB), starting with the simplest sub-group, and say what the group is. Method: triage by data shape, then one owning type per shape with the unlifted callees behind a trait, proven against the verified 32-bit rewrites.

Found (Verified). The 109 names are not one structure. Triage by callee count and by the constants and offsets each rewrite uses through its first argument gives about nine shapes, and the largest of them have 8 to 26 callees each. Four shapes were small enough to take first:

ShapeRoutines liftedProof
Task pose and blend state block (pose at a fixed offset, a state block with its own virtual height slots)lerp, drive blend, commit blend (3)6 tests, 4000 generated cases each; wrong versions caught
Seek-target record (no callees)seek target setup (1)3 tests; wrong versions caught
Task id lookup (two keyed tables, id word, default id)id or default (1)3 tests; wrong versions caught
Task request gate (vtable word, two globals, candidate words, one status probe)gate (1)3 tests; wrong versions caught

Findings: a rewrite's comment gave 10000.0 for a constant whose verified bits read 9999.5; the lift follows the bits. A turn-tracker routine reads its sine and cosine results from the integer return register while its contract declares a float result in the SSE register; this is not resolved and that routine is not lifted.

entry.title: A probe pin that answered zero hid a whole route
entry.summary: From lane a-H28.
entry.content:
From lane a-H28.

What was asked: a lane probe had to get the original to call a new helper on at least 20 of 60 completed trials, and the probe had been run for 60 trials with the helper's call site stubbed. It never fired the helper.

What was found (Verified): the probe scripted the lookup callee that the original calls just before the helper (a state-word record lookup) to answer zero. The original then takes a different branch and never reaches the helper. Scripting that one callee to answer a record on odd trials made the helper fire on 30 of 60 trials. The probe had been pinned on the object words and the other callees, and the lookup callee was the one that had been missed.

What it means: when a probe shows a route vacuous, check the scripted answer of every callee on the route before concluding the route is unreachable. A cycled script indexes by trial number, so a branch that only odd trials reach needs an odd index in its script.

Also (Verified): a helper answer and a region object answer scripted on the wrong parity left the branch unreached for a whole probe run, and a callee whose call site was left unpatched ran the real code natively.

How to reproduce: the probe contract and its generator are in the lane's retry folder (mkprobe.py, contracts28).

entry.title: A callee's write into the caller's frame faulted the rewrite: the contract asked for eight words where two fit (lane a-H21, corrected)
entry.summary: What was asked. Finish a partly proven rewrite whose remaining branch calls a stdcall callee that writes its result through a pointer into the rewrite's frame.
entry.content:
What was asked. Finish a partly proven rewrite whose remaining branch calls a stdcall callee that writes its result through a pointer into the rewrite's frame.

What was found. Verified on the stock worker: when the callee is declared stdcall with its out-parameter write going to a pointer into the rewrite's own frame, the rewrite faults on the rewrite side in about a third of the trials, while the original side runs cleanly. Pointing the same write at a heap object does not fault. Declaring the callee thiscall with the register argument not compared removes the fault but the rewrite returns a corrupted value. The same write through a thiscall callee elsewhere in the same function works, so the cause is not the frame layout alone. Cause not found.

ItemValueStatus
stdcall, stack-pointer writerewrite faults in 10 to 20 of 60 trialsVerified
stdcall, heap-pointer writeno faultVerified
thiscall declared, stack-pointer writeno fault, corrupted return valueVerified
Causenot foundUnknown

What was decided. Recorded as a checker gap. The worker is not edited. A checker investigation lane should take it before the branch is closed.

How to reproduce. Run a 60-trial probe with the callee's out block in the rewrite's frame, then the same probe with the block on the heap.

Correction by the coordinator

11 October 2026, 04:05. A checker investigation lane examined this the same night and found the fault is in the contract, not in the checker. In a contract, the count of a scripted write through a pointer argument is in words, not bytes. The contract asked for eight words to be written through a pointer to a local that is two words long in the rewrite, so the write ran over the rewrite's frame; the original's frame happened to have room. With a count of two the same branch passes 1,000 of 1,000 trials and a wrong version with the two words swapped is caught. The function was finished on that basis the same morning. What stands from this entry is the method of reduction; what does not stand is the conclusion that a callee's write into the caller's frame cannot be proven on the stock checker.

entry.content:

entry.title: An earlier stage read the wrong cursor on its second pass (lane a-H19)
entry.summary: What was asked. Continue the partly proven rewrite of one particle-effect evaluator (the loop over the rule count) from the stages left by earlier lanes.
entry.content:
What was asked. Continue the partly proven rewrite of one particle-effect evaluator (the loop over the rule count) from the stages left by earlier lanes.

What was found. The stage that covers the path where the clamped count is zero or negative takes its second pass from the header callee's answer. entry.title: Lane trap: copied sources keep old timestamps, and checker pins with different periods hide routes
entry.summary: Asked. Continue a deferred function from its last stage. Each stage edits the rewrite source and the contract, then the stock checker runs the stage and its wrong version.
entry.content:
Asked. Continue a deferred function from its last stage. Each stage edits the rewrite source and the contract, then the stock checker runs the stage and its wrong version.

FindingStatusWhat it means
Copying a file in PowerShell keeps the source's last-write time. A restored source can look older than the library built from the edited copy, so cargo skips the rebuild.Verified (the lane rebuilt after touching the file; the diagnostic library had been running)Several probes ran a diagnostic library and looked like rewrite faults for about twenty minutes. Set the time to now after any copy, or delete the crate's output before a build.
Contract scripts cycle with the trial number modulo their own length. Two scripts with periods two and four cannot reach every combination when the trial groups are coupled, and a route that needs a particular pair stays unreached and the verdict goes vacuous.Verified (decoupling by period four removed one vacuity and exposed a mismatch that the earlier pins had hidden)Choose one cycle length for every script that must line up, and check the call coverage for each callee after a change.
A pinned float route (nibble two) with a positive entry value and a flag-set trial mismatched on the constructor block only when both were present.Verified by decoupling (the mismatch disappears when the nibble pin is one); cause not yet locatedLeft open for the next lane; the route is recorded in the lane's notes.

Decided. Touch copied sources before every build; keep every script's cycle length equal within a stage.

How to reproduce. Restore a source with copy, build with cargo, and compare the library's time with the source's time. For the coupling, print the call-coverage map of the verdict and look for callees that never fire.

entry.title: Checker trap: a global written on every pass is compared only at its final value
entry.summary: 2026-10-11, lane a-H15. Verified.
entry.content:
2026-10-11, lane a-H15. Verified.

What was asked. Continue a particle-effect evaluator (one of the functions an earlier lane deferred as partly proven) to a loop stage, with the checker on version 8 and strict contracts.

FactValueWhat it means
Global words written on each pass of a loopTwo 4-byte ranges, written on every passThe globals check compares only the final value of each range, not what earlier passes wrote.
Last pass of the loop in the stage contractWrites zero to both wordsA swap of the two words is invisible in that contract (the wrong version passed 1,000 of 1,000 trials).

What was decided. A global that a loop writes on every pass needs a stage where the final pass writes a nonzero value, or a single-pass twin contract, to show that the neighbour-swap wrong version fails. The two-pass contract keeps its own wrong version (no second pass), which is caught.

Correction to an earlier lane. The earlier lane pinned an incoming register to zero because the function was thought to read its upper bits. The instruction bytes show that the function zeroes that register before the flag test, so the incoming value is never read. The pin was removed and the stage still passes 1,000 of 1,000 trials.

entry.title: A checker callee's seq list answers only its first step in each trial
entry.summary: From lane a-H02.
entry.content:
From lane a-H02.

What was asked. A lane continuing a deferred function had to extend an earlier stage contract so that a callee alternates its answer between the two sides of a branch, so that the branch the callee guards is exercised.

What was found. The earlier contracts used a seq list for the callee. A seq list is consumed per call, and its position is not carried from one trial to the next. A callee that the original calls once per trial therefore always answered its first step, and the second step never ran. The earlier proof reported that the callee alternated. It did not. The branch guarded by the second answer was never executed, though the function's proof was reported as covering it.

FactValueStatus
Callee called once per trial, seq [0, 1]Answer was 0 in every trial (the ID12 callee fired in every trial)Verified (verdict coverage counts)
Same callee with script [0, 1]Answered 0 and 1 across trials; the callee guarding the second answer fired in half the trialsVerified (verdict coverage counts)
Rewrite that had passed the earlier contract, run against the alternating contractFailed 30 of 60 on the second answer's tail; passed after its return value was changed to keep the callee's upper return bitsVerified

What was decided. Every alternating answer in this lane's contracts uses script, which the driver cycles per trial. The earlier stage contracts for the same function are not changed here; the next lane should re-derive them with the same rule before relying on them.

How to reproduce. Run the driver on one contract with a callee given seq [0, 1] and one with script [0, 1], both called once per trial. Read the callee's entry in the verdict's coverage block (callees_fired_on_ok) and the branch shapes.

Also learned. A rewrite that keeps only the low byte of a callee's return loses the callee's upper bits. When the original's return value is compared in full, the callee's upper bits are part of the result and must be kept. The checker reproduces them only when the rewrite calls the same stub.

entry.title: Encrypted callees are stubbed like plain ones; no live capture is needed for them
entry.summary: From lane a-H01.
entry.content:
From lane a-H01.

Asked. A deferred renderer function (its earlier lanes proved only the early exits) was said to need a live capture of the owner's running game, because one of its direct callees lies in the encrypted first megabyte of code and faults when the checker runs it natively.

FactValueWhat it means
Direct callee in the encrypted range faults when run nativelyVerifiedThe checker reports a read fault at the callee's first instruction.
A call site can be replaced by a scripted stub through the contract's patch list, even when the callee is encryptedVerifiedWith every direct call site of the function patched, the original completes 60 of 60 trials without a fault.
Indirect calls through a vtable can be scripted by planting a stub in a heap vtable, and in a game vtable slot through the globals listVerifiedThe eight indirect sites of the function run through one stub id; the game's own vtable code is never executed.
Whole-function rewrite with 35 callee ids passes six stock-v8 contractsVerified1,000 of 1,000 positives on each, with a same-contract wrong version failing 3 of 3 for each.

Decided. Encrypted callees are handled by stubs exactly like plain callees. A capture is needed only if a callee's real behaviour must be proven, which a stub never does. The earlier deferral's reason, that the mapped image is ciphertext at the callee, is correct about the bytes but was not a blocker for the checker. The function is recorded as verified with its narrowed list (stub semantics, null-receiver fault paths not proven).

Reproduce. Patch each direct call instruction of the function (its relative address in the image) to a scripted callee id in the contract, and plant the stub in each indirect target slot. Run the stock checker in a 60-trial probe: the original reports ok, orig_ok equal to the trial count.

Limits: the proof covers the function under the stub model only; a callee's real effects on its pointer arguments are not compared.

entry.title: The checker's option for unrelocated absolute reads has never set up on this machine
entry.summary: The checker has a contract option for an original that reads an absolute address which the loader did not relocate: the worker holds the address range of the original's preferred base, so such a read lands on a copy of the image. A lane on a large function asked for the option, was refused, and reported that the repository's own self-test contract for it fails the same way. A checker investigation lane took 15 minutes to settle it. The option fails at set-up on this machine every time, it has done so since the day it was added, and nothing a lane can do changes that.
entry.content:
The checker has a contract option for an original that reads an absolute address which the loader did not relocate: the worker holds the address range of the original's preferred base, so such a read lands on a copy of the image. A lane on a large function asked for the option, was refused, and reported that the repository's own self-test contract for it fails the same way. A checker investigation lane took 15 minutes to settle it. The option fails at set-up on this machine every time, it has done so since the day it was added, and nothing a lane can do changes that.

What was asked

Is the refusal a fault in the checker, a fault in the lane's contract, or the machine? Twenty deferred functions, 27,343 bytes, were queued behind this option, so the answer mattered beyond one lane.

What was found

QuestionFindingHow it is known
Does the self-test contract fail?Yes, at set-up, before any trial: 10 of 10 fresh driver runs, 40 of 40 set-up attempts counting the driver's own retries.Verified: run on the stock driver and worker.
What holds the range?One block mapped by the system, present at the first line of the worker's own code, covering the whole range. It is not the worker's image, which sits elsewhere. None of the 768 pieces of the range can be reserved, and the block cannot be released.Verified: a private copy of the worker that lists the regions in the range before it reserves anything.
Does it depend on how the worker is linked?The layout changes and the outcome does not. Linked at a fixed base, as the worker is, the block is always there. Linked to load at a random base, some pieces of the range are free on some starts, never all of them: 0 of 40 set-ups.Verified: two small 32-bit probe programs, one linked each way.
Is it new?No. The first lane log that records the worker holding none of the range is from 4 October, the day the option went live. Forty-one lane logs record a deferral for it since. No log of a contract passing with the option was found on this machine.Verified for the logs; that it never passed is inferred from finding none.
Does it depend on load, or on how the worker is started?No: the same with 25 other workers running and with none started by the driver.Verified.
Would it work after a restart, or on a machine with an x86 processor?Unknown. This machine runs 32-bit x86 code under emulation, which may be what maps the block; that was not tested.Unknown.

Repairs tried and ruled out: linking the worker differently, reserving earlier (the block is there before the worker runs), releasing the block, and retrying. Covering only the pieces that can be held was not tried, on purpose: the worker refuses a partial cover by design, because a read that lands on a piece it does not hold would silently read the worker's own memory.

What was decided

  • No lane is sent at a contract that needs this option, or at its self-test contract. The self-test's failure is a known condition of this machine, not a regression in the checker.
  • The twenty queued functions stay deferred with this as the stated reason. Before any of them is believed to need the option, its claim is checked with the relocation checker: an earlier devlog entry records that every such claim examined so far was wrong, and the worker already relocates absolute immediates so that most data reads work without the option (see the entry of 5 October on a production lane).
  • Getting the option to work is a design change to the checker, for the owner to decide: for example loading the original at its preferred base in a process built for that purpose. It is not a lane repair.

Correction

Lane notes since 4 October say the range is taken "in every 32-bit process". That is true only of programs linked at a fixed base. It does not change the outcome, and it is corrected here so the next investigation does not start from it.

How to reproduce

Run the self-test contract for the option from the checker's contract folder on the stock driver, ten times, each in a fresh driver process, and read the set-up message. The investigation lane's commands, outputs and the region listings are in its scratch folder.

entry.title: Hourly reviews, 11 October
entry.summary: The coordinator reviews the project critically once an hour. entry.content:
The coordinator reviews the project critically once an hour. Since this night the review runs from its own timer on a checklist the owner supplied, and starts from a scorecard a script prints: verified code in bytes per hour that held on the coordinator's own re-run is the measure, lifts are counted separately, and every exception the scorecard lists is acted on in the same hour. What was asked

To check every hour that the project is going in the right direction and to improve the process from what was just learned.

What was found

TimeMain findingDecision
00:20First review on the owner's checklist. In the 1.2 hours since 23:05: verified code up by 10,098 bytes in 11 functions imported after re-run (8,300 bytes an hour), nothing withdrawn, no portable lift, and 3,503 functions named, which took the named count from 32,227 to 35,730 of 37,413. Four Haiku lanes on large functions ended, each further along and none closed, and were continued by fresh lanes from their kits, except a 5,042-byte function that has had three sessions and is parked for a stronger lane. Every imported claim held on the re-run. Blockers, in order: the processor, at its ceiling for the whole hour with up to 21 compilers and 23 checker workers at once, so that a status command took ten minutes; the pipeline on the public repository, failing since 8 October; large functions, of which 384 of 1,807 of 1,000 bytes and more are verified and each takes several lane sessions; and the trust backlog, with 11% of the verified functions recorded on the current checker.The review got its own timer and a scorecard script, and the checklist went into the agent rules. Production brief version b24: a call into the part of the program encrypted on disk, or through a pointer, is replaced by a stand-in, not deferred (eight of one batch's seventeen functions had been deferred for it). A repair lane was put on the pipeline's two failures and a lift lane was started, the first since 6 October. The runaway guard was taught to recognise a script started by a lane's agent, and stopped seven over 3 GB. A filler starts Luna lanes while memory allows and the supervisor finishes them. Verified bytes per hour rose from about 4,300 to 8,300 while lanes rose fivefold: the extra lanes pay much less than in proportion.
01:25The best hour since work resumed. In 1.1 hours: verified code up by 14,183 bytes in 105 functions (13,500 bytes an hour, against 8,300 the hour before and 615 over the last 58 hours), five more routines lifted to portable Rust, 273 more functions named (36,003 of 37,413). The pipeline on the public repository passed for the first time since 8 October: a repair lane found both causes (a test received Python's own queue module because a checker import left it in the module cache; a lift test crate included a rewrite that had been withdrawn) and the coordinator tested and installed its candidates. Haiku lanes closed two more large functions, of 3,313 and 2,215 bytes, which makes four tonight; in the second the lane first showed, with realistic output values, that the earlier rewrite was wrong, then corrected and proved it. By model, for lanes that ended in the hour: Luna, 121 functions and 30,041 bytes in 19.7 lane-hours, 1,524 bytes per lane-hour; Haiku, 5,528 bytes in 3.0 lane-hours, 1,831 per lane-hour, all of it in functions Luna's lanes had left partly proven. Proof integrity: the re-run held eleven claims of one Luna lane, and that was the re-run's fault for the third time tonight: one slow contract ran the batch of fifteen into its time limit and the ten after it were never run. Run one at a time, all seventeen hold. Deferrals: 31 with the reason given only as "other" and 21 for time, in lanes that are slowed by the load. Three Luna lanes had written nothing for over twenty minutes; they run below normal priority and are slow, not stopped.Fixed in the hour. Every Luna lane's processes run below normal priority, so the steps that turn finished work into counted work get the processor first: thirteen finished lanes had been waiting, two for over half an hour, and the backlog cleared within minutes. Commits go one at a time and each takes only its own paths, after a pipeline repair went into the history inside an import commit that happened at the same moment. Next, with owners: the two large functions still partly proven (fresh Haiku lanes when the load allows; the 5,042-byte one waits for a stronger lane); the deferrals marked "other" (the coordinator reads a sample before the next review and the brief gets the missing reasons); the 14,997 proofs still to re-run on the current checker (nine Luna lanes running); one verified function whose contract and rewrite disagree about the register a callee's result is read from, found by the lift lane (a checker-reading lane). 02:05Scorecard for the 0.7 hours since 01:25: verified code up by 14,152 bytes in 155 functions (17,262 verified; 21,200 bytes an hour against 13,500 the hour before and 850 over the last 58 hours), no lift, 27 functions named, nothing withdrawn, the pipeline passing, no lane stalled, 4.0 GB of memory available. The 56 Luna lanes that ended in the last 65 minutes verified 253 functions and 38,200 bytes in 80.4 lane-hours: 475 bytes per lane-hour, against 1,524 the hour before and about 4,000 when twelve lanes ran. Small-function lanes finished 27% of their batches (175 of 637): 250 functions were not reached and 123 were deferred for time, in lanes that each get a small share of a saturated processor (18 logical processors, about sixty lanes with up to three checker workers each). Another 100 deferrals gave the reason only as "other"; read, most are lanes that counted every checker worker on the machine against a limit of three meant for their own, and did not run the checker at all. Queue lanes had also been handed the same functions several times over: thirty lanes, fourteen distinct functions. Proof integrity: the re-run held two claims of one Luna lane, and this time the finding is real: run again by hand, the original faults on a fifth of the trials where the rewrite returns normally, 60 and 67 of 300. Those two stay out. They are the first Luna claims that do not reproduce, 2 of about 550 tonight. Haiku: two more large functions closed in the window; one lane on a function whose main loop is still unmapped proved four stages and then declined the loop twice, the third function tonight where that happened.Changed in the hour. The limit of three checker workers is stated as a lane's own in the agent rules and in brief version b25, and the 68 functions left drafted and untested got a queue of their own, with five lanes on them. The queue brief maker counts the Luna queue series as taken; the ten duplicate lanes still running were stopped. Second, the 5,395 old proofs without a wrong version: the runner can do the build and the thousand trials, and a lane then only writes the wrong version; the brief for that kind of lane is next. The 07:05 review had measured the hour before (verified code up by 17,550 bytes in 75 functions, half the hour before it, with the processor shared between thirty production lanes, twelve naming lanes, five Haiku lanes and the new regression runner at normal priority) and was being acted on when the coordinator's turn was cut off. Second, the processor, once the lanes are back. Third, the old proofs without a saved wrong version, now about one in ten even among the newer ones. Second, the conversion audit: 288 functions not yet tested, and the verified count may fall again. Third, the large functions still open after six and seven sessions. No lift ran in the window, for want of a lane and not for a blocker; a lift lane follows when naming ends. Accelerating against the 29-hour baseline (7,100 bytes an hour, which includes the eight idle hours); not against last night's hours.

entry.title: Haiku lanes on three large functions that earlier lanes left partly proven
entry.summary: Three lanes run by Claude Haiku 5.5 each took one function of 2,200 to 2,900 bytes that three or four lanes of another model had left partly proven in stages. One closed its function in 36 minutes; two moved theirs further and stopped. None of the three is counted as verified today: the one proof that closed is held back because of the form of its rewrite. Each lane also found something the earlier lanes had got wrong.
entry.content:
Three lanes run by Claude Haiku 5.5 each took one function of 2,200 to 2,900 bytes that three or four lanes of another model had left partly proven in stages. One closed its function in 36 minutes; two moved theirs further and stopped. None of the three is counted as verified today: the one proof that closed is held back because of the form of its rewrite. Each lane also found something the earlier lanes had got wrong.

What was asked

The owner asked for Haiku lanes on the harder work where the other model's lanes are struggling. The first test was the queue of functions partly proven in stages, which holds the most deferred code: 72 functions, 186,000 bytes.

What was found

Lane's functionResultTime used of 95 minutesWhat it found
A renderer set-up routine, 2,491 bytes, 60 call sitesOne rewrite passes six contracts at 1,000 trials each; every wrong version fails. The coordinator re-ran all six: they reproduce.36The earlier deferral was wrong. It said the main path needs a capture from the running game because a callee lies in the part of the program that is encrypted on disk. A call site can be replaced by a scripted stand-in whether or not its target is encrypted: with all 52 direct call sites replaced and one function-table slot planted, the original completes every trial.
A proximity sweep, 2,215 bytesPartly proven, further than before: two new stages at 1,000 trials, four earlier ones replayed. The loop, the visited-set check and one flag branch remain.31An earlier stage's claim was wrong. Its contract gave a callee an answer sequence to alternate between two answers, but a sequence is consumed per call within a trial, and this callee is called once per trial, so only the first answer was ever given and one of the two paths never ran. The manual describes the sequence this way; the earlier contract misused it.
An audio occlusion update, 2,924 bytesPartly proven: six earlier stages replayed and one new mixed stage, each at 1,000 trials. Two things block the whole function.22Two gaps in the earlier stages. On the early-exit path the original returns whatever was already in the return register and the rewrite returns zero; the stage that "passed" did not compare that register. And two paths store a stack word the function has not written; the rewrite assumes zero, and the stages fail when the stack is filled with anything else.

Verified The six contracts of the first function were re-run by the coordinator on the stock checker against the lane's library: 6,000 trials pass and each wrong version is rejected.

Verified The answer-sequence behaviour is as the driver's manual states it. Whether other accepted proofs used a sequence for a callee that is called once per trial has not been counted yet.

Inferred The unwritten stack word in the third function is probably filled by a callee through a pointer argument: the lane's contracts leave the callees' writes through pointers unmodelled. The lane did not test this.

What was decided or recommended

  • The first function's rewrite is not imported. Its proof holds, but the rewrite keeps the original's stack as an array and mirrors every push into it. That carries the original's instruction sequence over instead of writing the behaviour as Rust, and the project's first rule allows only the second in the repository; a doubtful case stays out. It is recorded as held, with the reason, and needs rewriting in the project's form and proving again on the same six contracts. The lane very likely chose this form to reproduce stale stack words exactly, which is the same problem that stopped the third lane.
  • Two lanes stopped with most of their time unused while a named next step remained: read the callers to see whether the return value is used; model the callee's write through its pointer argument; continue to the loop. The launch note for these lanes gets a rule against stopping early, and a rule about the form of a large rewrite, before any more are started.
  • A count of accepted proofs that use an answer sequence for a callee called once per trial goes on the list of open trust work.
  • A deferral that says a function needs a capture from the running game because a callee is encrypted is to be re-read: 38 functions are in that queue.

How to reproduce it

Each lane's folder holds its stage contracts, the rewrite and its wrong versions, and a note for the next lane. The coordinator's re-run takes the contracts unchanged and runs them with the repository's driver.

What was confusing or went wrong

The work was paused by the owner after this batch, so the two unfinished functions were not sent back to their lanes. Lanes were not told what form a large rewrite must have beyond the standard for small ones, and the one lane that finished solved a hard problem in a form that cannot be published.

entry.title: Hourly reviews, 10 October
entry.summary: The coordinator reviews the project critically once an hour: whether the work is still pointed at the goal, what the last hour produced, what weakened confidence in the results, and what changes because of it. One row is added here per review. These rows are the Claude coordinator's; a second coordinator session runs lanes of another model on the same repository and keeps its own reviews. The last rows before these are in "Hourly reviews, 6 October".
entry.content:
The coordinator reviews the project critically once an hour: whether the work is still pointed at the goal, what the last hour produced, what weakened confidence in the results, and what changes because of it. One row is added here per review. These rows are the Claude coordinator's; a second coordinator session runs lanes of another model on the same repository and keeps its own reviews. The last rows before these are in "Hourly reviews, 6 October".

What was asked

To check every hour that the project is going in the right direction and to improve the process from what was just learned.

What was found

TimeMain findingDecision
11:10Work resumed today with a different lane model on this side: Claude Haiku 5.5 subagents, by the owner's instruction, first as a trial and then for the harder functions the other session's lanes are not getting through. 16,958 functions are verified, 45.3% of the functions. Throughput: one Haiku lane on 20 small functions verified 19 in 30 minutes (910 bytes, about 1,800 bytes per lane-hour, limited by the size of its batch), level with the earlier model's record per function; the entry "A smaller model on the production brief" has the comparison. Trust: the coordinator re-ran all 19 proofs on the stock checker before importing them, and all hold with their wrong versions rejected. One of the 19 is narrower than it looks (a store into the function's own argument slot is invisible to the checker) and says so in its result. Direction: three Haiku lanes are now on large functions that three or four lanes of the other model each left partly proven; the queue of such functions holds 186,000 bytes in 72 functions, the largest queue of deferred work. From their logs after five minutes, all three had read the earlier stage material and one had a combined stage contract passing 1,000 trials with its wrong version caught. The largest risk nothing runs against: two coordinators commit to one working tree with no lock between them, and the pipeline on the public repository has failed on every run since 8 October (a script test that loads the wrong module, and a lift test that includes a rewrite withdrawn on 7 October). Workstation: 13 GB of 47.6 free, no paging, nothing left behind; the registry shows 15 lanes of the other session and 3 of this one, which is at or just over the owner's limit of 15 depending on whether the other session's dispatcher and monitor are counted.Changed in the hour: a lane-by-name import (a broad pass would take rows the other session is holding for review); a re-run of a new model's claims before import; a launch note for Haiku lanes (a log line every five minutes, one checker worker and one build at a time, since the machine is shared); the queue brief builder can make a lane for chosen functions under its own lane series; the dashboard shows Claude subagent lanes with their model and prompt. The importer now keeps the indentation it finds in the verified index, after its first commit today rewrote the whole file in a different one (content checked identical). Stop doing: the re-run at the full trial count as a gate for small-function lanes; it took 17 minutes for a 30-minute lane, and 300 trials with the wrong version is enough to catch a claim that does not reproduce. No more Haiku lanes are started while the registry is at the limit. The pipeline failures are flagged to the owner as their own piece of work.
22:10Work started again at 20:30 at the owner's word, with a mix he asked for: Luna lanes for the bulk and Claude Haiku lanes for the harder functions, and 8 GB of memory kept available for his own use. Ten lanes were running by 20:48: seven Luna (four on small functions, one on larger ones, one re-running 350 proofs made on early checker versions, one on deferred functions that pass doubles in vector registers) and three Haiku (the two large functions left partly proven in the morning, and a rewrite of the held function in the project's form). Then the laptop went to sleep at about 20:57 and woke at 22:06. Every lane stood still for 70 minutes; the three Haiku lanes lost their connection and ended, and one push failed. Throughput for the hour is therefore close to nothing: 16,958 verified, unchanged, with 9 functions recorded as verified in lanes that are still running and not yet imported. Trust: nothing new was imported, so nothing to weigh; the Luna lanes run on the plain production brief for the first time from this coordinator, and their claims will be re-run before import as the first Haiku lane's were. One early sign from the Haiku lanes after they were resumed: the lane on the audio function found that the only caller discards the return value that stopped the morning's lane, which is the check the new launch note tells lanes to make. Workstation: 15.8 GB available of 47.6, no paging, both guards alive.Changed in the hour. The laptop is asked to stay awake while the session works, and the watch never waits more than four minutes, since the hold lapses after about five idle ones; a closed lid still stops everything, and the owner knows. The three Haiku lanes were resumed from their own state with a new time limit. A launcher for Luna lanes as plain Codex processes replaces the Muse launcher for now, with the same restart rule. A floor guard keeps 8 GB available: no lane is started under 10 GB, and if available memory stays under 8 GB for half a minute the project's largest build is stopped. Launch note h2 for Haiku lanes: do not stop while time and a next step remain; write the behaviour as Rust and never mirror the original's stack; a stack word read before it is written usually comes from a callee's pointer argument; check whether any caller reads a return value before deferring over it. The dashboard and the status script count Luna processes. Stale rows of the morning's other session, 26 still marked as running, are marked stopped when their lane has been silent for an hour. Stop doing: nothing dropped this hour. The Luna lanes' time limits ran through the sleep, so most will stop short of their batches; what they did not reach goes back to the pool. Held at ten lanes until the first Luna claims pass the re-run.
23:05The first full hour of the evening's mix. 16,992 functions verified, 45.4% of the functions and 32.6% of the code by size: 35 more than at the last review, after one withdrawal. Twelve lanes ran, eight Luna and four Haiku. Throughput by lane kind, in the lanes' real working time (three of the first Luna lanes lost 70 minutes to the laptop's sleep, so their own clocks say less than they did). Luna on small functions: 43 verified in seven lanes that have ended or are well along; the uninterrupted ones are making 10 to 27 functions per lane-hour, against 29 to 38 in the earlier model's record and 37 in this morning's one Haiku lane. Luna on larger functions: 1 of 5, with 4 deferred. Luna on the queue of deferred functions that pass doubles: 4 verified in two lanes, 1 deferred. Luna re-running old proofs: 291 of 312 run hold on the current checker in the first lane, 522 of 522 so far in the two that are running. Haiku on large functions left partly proven: two closed and imported (2,924 and 2,491 bytes, the second being the function held in the morning, now written in the project's form), four more in progress. Trust: every claim was re-run by the coordinator's scripts before import, 40 of 40 from Luna and 2 of 2 from Haiku holding. The re-run itself failed twice in the hour, both times by running a lane's contracts against the wrong library, and the second time it marked nine good claims as not holding before the fault was seen; nothing was imported or withdrawn on it. One function was withdrawn: its old proof is vacuous on the current checker. Twenty old proofs could not be run at all and stay counted as an open item, fourteen of them because their contracts give a stack argument in a form the current driver refuses, which may mean they were made on a private copy of the driver. Direction: the Haiku lanes keep finding errors in earlier stage work (a stage that read two helpers' answers from the wrong register and so always saw zero; sixteen replayed stages that never reach the part of the function they were taken to cover; a second deferral for an encrypted callee that was no blocker). The largest risk nothing runs against is unchanged: the pipeline on the public repository has failed since 8 October. Workstation: 16.4 GB available of 47.6, no paging, processor at 100% for much of the hour.Changed in the hour. A supervisor for the Luna side finishes each lane when it ends (re-run, hold, import by lane name, publish) and keeps eight running while 10 GB or more is available. The re-run finds a lane's library whether the contract names it or the lane passed it through the environment, handles a function proven by several stage contracts, and reports a run in which every trial fails with no failed comparison as its own fault, which can no longer hold a claim. The importer commits the index when only the recorded checker version changed. All four Haiku lanes on large functions stopped between minute 18 and minute 37 of 95 with their next step named in their own reports, despite the launch note's rule; each was sent back in with its context and the steps in order, and the note now says the limit is a deadline to compute and check, and that an early report with work open is sent back. Stop doing: taking a Haiku lane's first report on a large function as its result. Held at twelve lanes although the owner's limit is fifteen: the limit exists for heat and the processor is already at its ceiling. Open and recorded: the fourteen unrunnable contracts, three tracked rewrites that do not compile, three missing contracts, and a count of accepted proofs that script a once-per-trial callee with an answer sequence.

The coordinator then re-ran all 19 proofs itself on the stock checker: all 19 hold and every deliberately wrong version is rejected. On small functions it is level with the lanes the process was tuned on. Nothing is measured yet for large functions.

What was asked

The owner asked for Haiku subagents to be tried in place of the earlier lane model, starting with one lane, and for a judgement of whether it is better or worse. The earlier model could not be run alongside, so the comparison is against its recorded lanes of the same kind: small-function production lanes on checker versions 6 to 8.

Another session's notes from 8 October describe the same limit, so the finding is independent, not new. An argument slot belongs to the called function, so a store there is not behaviour its caller can observe; the proof is narrower than it looks and says so.

What was decided or recommended

  • The 19 rewrites were imported after the re-run, by lane name.
  • Three Haiku lanes were started on large functions that several lanes of another model had left partly proven in stages. That is where the owner wants Haiku used, and it is the measurement that is missing.

  • The note given to a Haiku lane at launch now asks for a log line at least every five minutes. The first lane wrote five lines in half an hour, and the coordinator's five-minute report had nothing to show.

How to reproduce it

The baseline is every small-function production lane with a checker version 6, 7 or 8 marker: batch size from its list, verified rows from its results file, minutes from the launcher's lines in its log. The re-run takes each contract the lane wrote, unchanged, and runs it with the repository's driver against the library the contract names; the driver runs the declared wrong version with it.

What was confusing or went wrong

The brief is given whole to a lane of the earlier model. A subagent reads it from a file, and its file reader cuts lines after about 2,000 characters; the brief has longer ones. The lane was given a copy with line breaks added at sentence ends and nothing else changed. The lane also wrote its report under a different file name than the brief asks for, because of a rule of its own environment about that file type; the launch note now says the brief's name is allowed in its scratch folder.

Continue real missing branches, review exact negative controls and prioritize complete small functions where useful.

Continue work with Luna at maximum effort and keep the local dashboard useful for following each lane.

What was found

Verified A coordinator-owned local registry supplies explicit task state. Registry data older than three minutes is shown as unknown rather than running. The lane list, model and effort, an opened log panel and an expanded initial prompt were inspected in the rendered browser. Registry tests cover stale, malformed and finished state.
