Keep the process discovery for existing launchers and add native lane state alongside it. Label unavailable task memory, distinguish the paused Muse supervisor from coordinator-managed lanes, and include native lanes in history and status updates. Regression lanes show proofs checked; reproducing a historic positive result without a current negative control does not claim new verification.

Run the dashboard and status scripts with fresh explicit native lane registry entries. Open each lane card, inspect its log and prompt, then make the registry stale and confirm that running state disappears. Run the dashboard and registry tests in the coordinator test directory.

entry.title: A stack leak hiding in an event-handler update
entry.summary: One of this lane's two verified functions leaks four bytes of stack every time it takes its numeric-entry path, because it calls a caller-cleanup helper without the cleanup. Verified The leak shifts the function's own frame, so its epilogue restores the wrong registers and returns with the stack pointer low; in the game that path presumably never fires with a nonzero entry, since the cookie check would then fail.
entry.content:
One of this lane's two verified functions leaks four bytes of stack every time it takes its numeric-entry path, because it calls a caller-cleanup helper without the cleanup. Verified The leak shifts the function's own frame, so its epilogue restores the wrong registers and returns with the stack pointer low; in the game that path presumably never fires with a nonzero entry, since the cookie check would then fail.

What was asked

Rewrite two medium-to-large input-event functions in Rust and prove each rewrite identical to the original with the checker, spending most of the effort on the proof contract.

What was found

Verified Both functions verified at one thousand trials each with all mutants caught. The smaller one refreshes a timer and then programs event-handler objects down one of three paths; the larger one appends about thirty input events and tags each object. Its register-indirect calls go through the import slot for the thread-id function, whose on-disk value is a placeholder the loader patches at startup, so the contract plants the stub there.

Verified The smaller function's numeric path parses a string, scales it, and passes it on, but never cleans the parser's argument off the stack. Each numeric entry in its four-entry loop costs four more bytes. The proof leaves the stack-pointer check off and says so; the leaked slots hold only values already observed as call arguments.

Verified The larger function is three bytes longer than the inventory says: the listed size ends mid-instruction, before the final store and return.

What was decided or recommended

Both rewrites were accepted with the leak documented in the proof record rather than reproduced. A useful follow-up for the lint tool: warn when a contract's global address looks like a full address instead of an image offset, which cost this lane its first probe. The checker's manual also describes per-call answer steps as pairs where the driver accepts only single values; the pair form is what the worker receives after resolving.

How to reproduce it

Run this lane's two contracts from its scratch folder with the stock checker driver and worker; each passes one thousand trials with its deliberately wrong version failing. The leak is visible by auditing every push and cleanup in the smaller function: all balance except the single parser call on the numeric path.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first rewrite of the smaller function fell through from the parked branch into the second object's code, adding two extra calls per trial; aligning the two call logs showed the exact divergence and the original's jump over that code. Small aligned value cycles also locked the string path out entirely until they were replaced with incommensurate periods. One store global was missing from the larger contract's declared ranges and the undeclared-write check caught it on the first probe.

entry.title: Lifting the replay bar: one prefix, four shapes, and a backend that commutes
entry.summary: 6 October 2026 — lane l-free12 (Muse)
entry.content:
6 October 2026 — lane l-free12 (Muse)

Asked: lift the eighteen verified free routines named replay_bar_* to portable Rust, working out from the rewrites which data they share and what the group is. Found: a playback timeline scrubber — a time range, a slot total, a table of stamped slot entries, selection state, marker bounds, hit rectangles, a cursor, a clock link and bar geometry — plus three more shapes under the same prefix: a notifier control, a clock-blend free function with no this, and a deferred layout cell. Seventeen routines lifted and proven against their rewrites (about 110,000 comparisons, every wrong lift caught); the layout cell is a different object with seventeen callees and waits for its own lane.

What the session taught

  • Triage by descriptor shape earns its keep again: one word offset is the bar's seconds float to one routine and a different object's inner pointer to another. One offset with two meanings means two types.
  • Neighbour runs are not instances until the hashes say so: all eighteen normalised bodies differ, so each routine stands alone — including two pairs that read like one routine twice.
  • The code generator commutes spilled float multiplies, and NaN payloads observe the destination lane. The differential test caught it; the fix pins both multiply sides with black_box in the lift. Random-bit floats are too weak a guard for this class — geometry fields now cycle the edge corpus.
  • Routines that call through pointers they read from memory need genuine stub addresses planted into fake virtual tables; call order across all callees then compares through one unified log per side.

No routine in the group reaches the operating system: every callee is game-internal, so no platform trait was needed. Full detail, with per-routine evidence, is in the lane report under .artifacts/scratch/l-free12/report.md.

entry.title: Naming dummy tasks: a 12-slot vtable of their own
entry.summary: One hundred fifty consecutive task-system functions were named: 62 at high confidence and 83 at medium, with 5 left unnamed. The main finding is that the nine dummy-task classes share a 12-slot virtual table with its own layout, not the layout of the regular task classes, and each slot's role was worked out from the code.
entry.content:
One hundred fifty consecutive task-system functions were named: 62 at high confidence and 83 at medium, with 5 left unnamed. The main finding is that the nine dummy-task classes share a 12-slot virtual table with its own layout, not the layout of the regular task classes, and each slot's role was worked out from the code.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of 150 consecutive unnamed game functions, working out what the group is about first and then naming each one, with high, medium or low confidence.

What was found

Verified The batch holds five groups: the dummy-task family and its helpers, the jumping-task family, one ambient-task class with its table helpers, explosion audio slots, and animation-request bookkeeping.

Verified The dummy-task virtual table has 12 slots. Slot zero destroys, one slot ticks the cheap simulation, one formats debug text (its per-class format strings name flee targets, watched events and scenario positions), one builds the real task when the dummy is promoted, and one gates aborting on priority. Two slots exist only for the dead variant: a camera-visibility check and corpse presentation.

Verified One listed function is not a function at all: it is the jump table of the neighbouring factory that builds dummy tasks by number. The factory itself was named from its eight allocation branches.

Inferred Two widely reused shared labels look wrong: the routine that frees deleting objects is labelled as a script native, and a common call target carries a weapon native label. Both sit in the encrypted region so neither could be checked directly.

What was decided or recommended

Names follow the established project style: destructors and constructors under their class names, abort and clone under the standard task vocabulary, and plain helper names where no class owns the code. The next naming lane covering nearby code should check three mislabelled promotion functions currently filed as unrelated constructors, and the pending weapon-info layout will unlock three explosion-audio helpers left unnamed here.

How to reproduce it

Read the executable through the mapped image, never the raw file at a mapped address, and confirm the mapping by decoding one known constructor first. Dump each class virtual table from the data section and cross-check every slot against prior lane names; decode every small function fully and skim large ones by callee names and referenced strings.

What was confusing or went wrong

The subsystem clustering was wrong for part of the batch: functions labelled audio turned out to be jumping and ambient task code, while the true audio group sat elsewhere. The base abort implementation shared between dummy and regular tasks lives in the encrypted region, so that alias rests on behaviour of the overrides, not on reading the shared code.

entry.title: Two in a hundred old proofs do not reproduce on the current checker, and a night of audits in one table
entry.summary: Between midnight and eight in the morning on 6 October the checker gained two versions and five separate audits ran against the verified tree. This entry puts their results side by side, because the last one changes what the others mean: the weakness that matters most is not any one blind spot but the age of most proofs.
entry.content:
Between midnight and eight in the morning on 6 October the checker gained two versions and five separate audits ran against the verified tree. This entry puts their results side by side, because the last one changes what the others mean: the weakness that matters most is not any one blind spot but the age of most proofs.

What was asked

Each audit asked the same question of a different part of the tree: is there a way for a rewrite to be wrong and still pass, and if so, how many verified rewrites are wrong that way?

What was found

AuditIn scopeResultStatus
Pointer arguments the proof skips (the buffer behind them was not compared)2,992 verified functions, 4,633 call sites22 rewrites handed a callee something other than the original does and are repaired and proved again; 3 are withdrawn with a written repair; about 40 candidates turned out not to be wrongVerified: every case settled by a run, with the old behaviour run as the wrong version
Input words whose description used a key the driver did not know (it gave them random bits)73 verified proofsAll 73 hold under the contract their authors meantVerified: proved again on the stock checker
Where inside a declared range a global variable is written (not compared before checker version 8)1,578 verified proofsNo misplaced write in any of them. 714 of the proofs never changed a global in any trial. 598 of those have been sorted: 581 belong to functions that only read their globals, and 17 write one on a path no trial reached; the other 116 are not sorted yetVerified: 400 re-run with one-word ranges, 1,172 re-run unchanged on version 8
Proofs an audit lane could not reproduce after adding its own snapshots28All 28 reproduce exactly as recorded; the audit's snapshots read through pointers that are invalid in some trialsVerified: run on the proving lanes' own libraries and on fresh builds
Old proofs re-run unchanged on the current checker (a by-product of the third audit)1,17724 do not reproduce: about 2%Verified for the count; the causes are in the next table

The 24 that did not reproduce

What happened on the current checkerCountWhat it means
Vacuous: a callee never fired on a completed trial4The checker that accepted them had no such rule; the proof compared nothing about those calls
Calls or heap differ4Not yet explained; two are a not-a-number's payload
Call log cut short (more than a thousand calls attempted, 256 logged)2The earlier checker passed a truncated log; the calls past the limit were never compared
The current driver cannot load the contract4Contract shapes that later versions stopped accepting; cannot be re-run without rewriting the contract
The tracked rewrite does not compile2The file in the repository is not the file that was proved
The tracked rewrite is missing or cut short5An index row without a usable file
The rewrite faults, or writes an undeclared global2Not yet explained
One trial in a hundred differs in a not-a-number's payload1The compiler had reordered a float addition; repaired with the order pinned and proved again

None of these was found by looking for it. They appeared because 1,177 proofs happened to be re-run for another reason.

Why this is the larger finding

Checker version of the proof of recordVerified functionsBytes
1 and 24,470315,600
31,945255,200
44,614649,900
53,349573,700
62,135607,000
7 and 847869,000

Two thirds of the verified functions were accepted by checker versions 1 to 4, before the checker refused vacuous proofs, before a deliberately wrong version was required for every function, and before most of what it can now observe existed. The project's plan says the regression between waves is the re-run of every rewrite under the current checker. That stopped being done when rewrites began to be committed on every five-minute tick. If the rate in this sample holds, about 220 of those 11,029 functions have a proof that would not be accepted today. Inferred: the sample was not random (it was the proofs with a wide global range), so the true rate may differ.

What was decided

  • A standing regression: lanes that take the verified functions oldest checker version first, 350 at a time, and re-run each proof of record unchanged on the current checker. A proof that holds is replaced by the same rewrite and contract proved on the current version. A proof that is vacuous, fails, or cannot be run is recorded with its evidence, and the coordinator withdraws it from the verified count.
  • Two lane starts in twelve go to it from the next supervisor window, taken from one lift start and one start on the largest functions.
  • Withdrawals are made on a run, or on a reading the coordinator has confirmed on both sides, never on a lane's reading alone. In this night's audits a reading lane called 16 rewrites wrong and was right about 10; an audit's snapshot run called 23 wrong and was right about 7; and the coordinator's own second opinions on ten cases were right five times.

How to reproduce

The scope lists and the re-run lanes' tables are in the audit lanes' folders under the scratch area, which is not published. The counts by checker version come from the verified index (rewrites/verified/index.json, field checker) and the function inventory's sizes. The regression lanes' briefs are written by a script in the coordinator's folder that takes the oldest proofs first.

What was confusing

The audit that looked hardest for wrong rewrites produced the most false alarms, and the plainest one, running old proofs again without changing anything, produced the finding. A stricter checker does not make old verdicts stricter; only running them again does.

entry.title: Three stack bugs in the original, found by proving rewrites
entry.summary: A production batch of six task-system functions yielded four verified rewrites and two partial proofs, and the two partial proofs are the interesting part: in three of the six functions the original code itself cleans up the stack wrongly after some calls, so those paths return into garbage and crash. The proofs had to be split into completing paths, which pass, and faulting paths, which are demonstrated crashing.
entry.content:
A production batch of six task-system functions yielded four verified rewrites and two partial proofs, and the two partial proofs are the interesting part: in three of the six functions the original code itself cleans up the stack wrongly after some calls, so those paths return into garbage and crash. The proofs had to be split into completing paths, which pass, and faulting paths, which are demonstrated crashing.

What was asked

Rewrite six neighbouring task-system functions in Rust and prove each rewrite identical to the original on the checker, with at least a thousand trials and a deliberately wrong version per function.

What was found

  • Verified Four functions proved fully: two task initialisers, one virtual route-following step with lazy global caches and a double-precision helper call, and one accept-or-reject check with two virtual calls.
  • Verified In three functions the original mis-cleans the stack on some paths: one never cleans a three-word call (its flag and out-word are then read back from never-written slots, so they are always stale), one pops four bytes too many per report call and per marker trio, and one pops twelve too many around its script block. Each faulting path was run and observed crashing; no completing rewrite can match a crashing original, so these are recorded as passing stages plus fault demonstrations.
  • Verified Three functions read a never-written aligned-frame scratch slot into an output word. Under the checker's zero stack fill that word is zero, which is what the rewrites store; each proof documents it.
  • Inferred The faulting paths look like dead or defensive code, or paths the game's own state never reaches: each smells like a caller/callee declaration mismatch, and each crashes in the real game too, since no callee behaviour can balance the arithmetic.

What was decided or recommended

The two affected functions are recorded as partly proven: the completing-paths stage passes on the stock checker with mutants caught, and a retry kit (full rewrite, stage contract and verdict, fault analysis, fault-demonstration contract) waits in the lane folder. The next lane should read the fault analysis first and decide between accepting the stage and attempting fault parity, which is expected to be fragile. A reusable lesson: when the original faults on some trials, check the caller's own stack arithmetic before suspecting the contract — the bytes of one cleanup instruction settled two of these cases.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's stage contracts for the two affected functions (all completing paths pass), then run the retry folder's full contracts, which steer trials into the faulting paths and show the original faulting where the rewrite completes. The lane log and report name every file.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two self-inflicted faults cost the most time. First, a wrong nibble in a contract's function field sent a run at the wrong bytes; the contract linter catches this in a second and should run before every first attempt. Second, pin phases that looked independent combined to make a callee path unsatisfiable, producing a vacuous verdict; aligning one pin to odd trials fixed it. A transient build lock from a stale handle was fixed by removing the built file after confirming no process held it.

entry.title: Production lane: 28 text-field functions verified, two held by a global-fill gap
entry.summary: A production batch of 30 small input-ui functions finished with 28 verified on the stock checker and two deferred: scripted values for game globals demonstrably failed to reach those two functions' reads, while the checker's own control contracts pass, so the rewrites are kept for a later re-run.
entry.content:
A production batch of 30 small input-ui functions finished with 28 verified on the stock checker and two deferred: scripted values for game globals demonstrably failed to reach those two functions' reads, while the checker's own control contracts pass, so the rewrites are kept for a later re-run.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of 30 neighbouring text-field functions in Rust and prove each rewrite identical to the original with the project checker, one contract per function, each with a deliberately wrong version that must fail.

What was found

  • Verified 28 of 30 functions pass 1,200 trials each with a caught wrong version, covering child selection, key classifiers, cursor and mode handling, virtual-call forwarding, float scaling and validation, and a five-record text builder.
  • Verified Eleven functions return through byte-only writes that preserve the upper 24 bits of the last value in the register. Small test inputs hide this; only values above one byte catch it.
  • Verified One builder function leaks its call windows on purpose and its finalizer pops thirteen words. A probe with the wrong pop size faults exactly as predicted; with the right size it completes balanced.
  • Verified A computed tail jump through a virtual table verifies with a normal stub. A no-cleanup stub models the wrong callee shape and fails the stack-pointer check.
  • Verified Two functions could not be steered: the values scripted for the game globals they read never took effect (pinned and random fills alike), while the checker's own global-read controls pass on the same worker. Their rewrites and contracts are kept for a re-run.
  • Verified A suspected calling-convention bug in one function turned out to be the lane's own arithmetic slip. A probe showing clean completion forced a recount before anything was reported.

What was decided or recommended

Ship the 28 verified rewrites. Re-run the two deferred functions once scripted global values reach reads; their contracts need no changes. Any lane whose wrong version passes on a function that reads game globals should check whether its fills actually land before trusting the proof.

How to reproduce it

Each function has a contract and a verdict file in the lane scratch folder; the generators, table-extraction scripts and the probes (including the global-fill controls) sit beside them. The two deferred functions reproduce as a passing correct run with a passing wrong version, and a vacuous verdict with unfired callees, respectively.

What was confusing or went wrong

The global-fill gap cost the most time: every link in the chain (driver request bytes, worker source order, setup parsing, relocations) reads correctly, the controls pass, yet the two functions behave as pristine. The root cause is still unknown. Separately, one mutant passed sixty trials because the callee script cycled the identical sequence as the stack input; offsetting one of them caught it at once.

entry.title: Naming 150 shader, targeting and task functions
entry.summary: Named 147 of 150 consecutive game functions covering a vehicle paint shader effect, the ped targeting object, navmesh route-following tasks, vehicle enter and exit tasks, and a set of placeholder task constructors.
entry.content:
Named 147 of 150 consecutive game functions covering a vehicle paint shader effect, the ped targeting object, navmesh route-following tasks, vehicle enter and exit tasks, and a set of placeholder task constructors.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name with confidence for each function in the batch, working out what each group does first, using strings, imports, known callers, class tables and verified rewrites as evidence.

What was found

Verified Joining over a thousand earlier naming proposals with the symbol table recovers the task vtable protocol: clone, task id, make abortable, create first and next sub task, and control sub task sit in fixed slots across the whole task family.

Verified Six targeting methods were named directly from verified rewrite documents, and nine placeholder task constructors were identified by reading the class tables each one installs.

Inferred The vehicle enter and exit tasks run a status machine: each class has a jump table mapping status numbers to readable names, a counter that advances the status, a setter for it, and a builder that creates the sub task for the current status.

Inferred Vtable slots with the same number can mean different things in different class families: the slot that selects a sub task id in combat tasks holds the whole sub task builder in vehicle tasks. Behaviour, not slot number, decided those names.

What was decided or recommended

Follow the recovered slot protocol for future task batches, but verify giant overrides against the constructors they call before trusting the slot. Reading a class table from the image settles constructor identity and exposes stubbed slots a sibling class never overrode.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each function through the mapped image, resolve callees against the merged symbols, prior lane names and verified rewrite index, collect referenced strings and constants, read the class tables for constructor and slot attribution, then name from the strongest signal per function.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two shell commands failed on quoting before all dumping moved into scripts. One assumed slot transfer was wrong: the sibling shader class leaves the slot a stub, so the name came from the function's own behaviour instead.

entry.title: Lifting the input-ui holders: ten free functions, four shapes
entry.summary: What was asked: lift the 35 verified routines sharing the input-ui name prefix, a group chosen by name rather than by class, and find what data they actually share. (Verified: all 35 rewrites triaged by signature, doc comment and global/callee use.)
entry.content:
What was asked: lift the 35 verified routines sharing the input-ui name prefix, a group chosen by name rather than by class, and find what data they actually share. (Verified: all 35 rewrites triaged by signature, doc comment and global/callee use.)

What was found: the prefix is a pipeline, not a structure. The 35 routines span about twenty data shapes. The largest real shape is the element holder family: every holder opens with a table pointer and an id word whose low bits are stamped from a global counter and whose middle bits are folded from two polled answers. Three constructor routines proved to be byte-identical instances of one routine by diff. A sibling verified batch names the family as a generic callback-holder template with verified constructors, copy constructors and teardown, which are the natural next lift. (Verified: file diffs; sibling file headers.)

What was decided: lift the holder family (six routines as four methods on one owning type), plus the state-record copy, the bounds accumulator, the float predicate and the entry scanner: ten routines proven against their rewrites with 24,591 differential comparisons and eleven deliberately wrong versions caught, with 36 host tests. Small unrelated shapes were kept in separate modules rather than merged into a drawer. The remaining 25 routines were ranked by outside-call count for the next lane; the mode-table pair and the state initialiser are the easiest next proofs. (Verified: test runs on the 32-bit target and the 64-bit host.)

Method notes for the next free-function group: hash neighbour bodies before lifting once; run the differential suite in release mode when a rewrite relies on wrapping arithmetic; compare float-carrying logs bit for bit because NaN never equals itself; and plant virtual slots as real tables pointing at recording stubs. Full detail is in the lane report.

entry.title: Naming combat, cover and effects functions: slot 24 selects the subtask id
entry.summary: One hundred fifty consecutive functions were named 117 ways, and the main result is a new virtual-slot meaning: slot 24 on combat subtasks picks which subtask to build next by type id, pairing with the subtask factory at slot 25 found earlier.
entry.content:
One hundred fifty consecutive functions were named 117 ways, and the main result is a new virtual-slot meaning: slot 24 on combat subtasks picks which subtask to build next by type id, pairing with the subtask factory at slot 25 found earlier.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for a batch of consecutive unnamed game functions, mostly combat-ai and cover tasks with some effects code at the end, working from strings, called functions, virtual-table slots and prior lane names.

What was found

Verified Slot 24 on every combat subtask returns a task type id, from constant ids for charge and execute subtasks to weapon-state and decision-maker queries for fire and retreat subtasks.

Verified Slot 22 has no single meaning even inside one family: sibling overrides abort, retarget, swap aim nodes or relink posture nodes, and the cover family uses a different argument count, so each override needed its own name.

Verified Four functions the inventory listed as unreferenced were placed into their virtual tables by scanning read-only data for pointers to them, which also confirmed their classes through type records.

Verified Twenty-one task type ids were read from constant stubs, and a sweep of every such stub in the binary resolved several more referenced ids while leaving six still unidentified.

What was decided or recommended

Slot 24 is called select subtask id and slot 22 is named per function. The type-id getter keeps the newest lanes spelling until the project picks one of the two spellings in use. The next lane should map the effects data sections to their lookup tables, identify six unknown task ids, and run the pointer scan on every batch since inventory tags miss entries.

How to reproduce it

Read code through the mapped executable image, never the raw file at a mapped address. Decode one known constant stub first to confirm the mapping, gather per-function evidence of calls, strings and constants into one table, cross virtual slots against prior lane names, and scan read-only data for pointers to anything apparently unreferenced before leaving it unnamed.

What was confusing or went wrong

A redirected output file came out in an encoding that read back garbled, so later reads used the structured evidence file instead. Two commands ran slowly under load but delivered complete results. The two competing spellings of the type-id getter took a three-way check that settled nothing, and time ran out on the collision-dispatch family and the effects table mapping, which were documented rather than guessed.

entry.title: Running the skipped pointers that could not be read
entry.summary: Asked: 377 verified functions had a call whose pointer argument the proof skips and whose buffer nobody could read. A reading lane had studied every skipped pointer in the original code and left these undecided. We ran them with the buffer compared instead: a snapshot of the words behind each skipped pointer at each call, 300 trials on the stock checker, then narrowing and per-site reruns for everything that failed.
entry.content:
Asked: 377 verified functions had a call whose pointer argument the proof skips and whose buffer nobody could read. A reading lane had studied every skipped pointer in the original code and left these undecided. We ran them with the buffer compared instead: a snapshot of the words behind each skipped pointer at each call, 300 trials on the stock checker, then narrowing and per-site reruns for everything that failed.

Found: 238 functions settled without repair. In 69 the rewrite hands over the same words. In 120 the buffer is uninitialised at the call, so there is nothing stored to compare. In 49 the words differ but the callee writes before it reads or never touches the buffer, so the earlier proof stands. One function was wrong and is repaired and re-proved: a wrapper that dropped its entry register and passed zero where the original passes a pointer the nested converter reads through. 22 more functions show the same shape, stored words differing where the callee reads first, and are specified for repair. The rest are deferred with reasons: sites that cannot be snapshotted, callees in the encrypted region, diffs that stay hidden, and a cluster that diverges only in termination with or without snapshots, which lives in the base proof rather than the buffer.

Decided: running settles what reading could not, and two rerun tricks do most of it. Rerunning with a zero stack fill turns every uninitialised word into a match, so any remaining diff is stored. The patterned fill is exactly invertible, so pattern reruns classify words by arithmetic. Both were validated against controls. The repair backlog is ordered by callee verdict: read-first sites first.

Reproduce: the lane folder holds the list, all run verdicts, the consolidation script, and the per-function results; the one repair ships with its contract, verdict and caught mutant.

entry.title: Production batch: three fire-task dispatches verified, plus a driver output trap
entry.summary: Three neighbouring fire-task dispatch routines (about one thousand bytes each) were rewritten in Rust and verified against the originals with twelve hundred trials each, including fault-parity and wrong-version runs. The batch also exposed a tooling trap worth knowing: the checker driver writes its run summary to results.json next to itself, which silently overwrote this lane's deliverable of the same name twice.
entry.content:
Three neighbouring fire-task dispatch routines (about one thousand bytes each) were rewritten in Rust and verified against the originals with twelve hundred trials each, including fault-parity and wrong-version runs. The batch also exposed a tooling trap worth knowing: the checker driver writes its run summary to results.json next to itself, which silently overwrote this lane's deliverable of the same name twice.

What was asked

Rewrite three medium-sized routines from the same task-dispatch module and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original, with contracts that script every outgoing call (including calls into the encrypted first megabyte of code and calls through object function tables) and a deliberately wrong version per routine that must fail.

What was found

  • Verified All three routines verified on the stock checker with no deferrals: one over four staged contracts (including fault-parity trials for a re-initialisation path), one over three stages, one in a single contract. Every wrong version failed on exactly the word it changed.
  • Verified The driver summary clobber is real and repeatable: each run replaced the lane's results file with run statistics. Both losses were reconstructed from the per-contract verdict files. Redirecting driver output to a subdirectory avoids it.
  • Verified The float gates in this family are equality tests, not NaN tests. A compare-against-zero followed by a parity-tested flag check branches exactly when the value is not positive zero (any nonzero value or NaN takes the same side). A direct equality comparison in the rewrite matches bit-exactly.
  • Verified Direct calls into the encrypted region intercept and script normally, confirming earlier lanes; no routine here needed deferring for that reason.

What was decided or recommended

  • Consider renaming the driver's summary output so it cannot collide with lane deliverables, or briefing lanes to redirect driver output. Until then, a running lane's results file should not be read as authoritative mid-run.
  • Lanes modelling flag-based float branches should work out the parity logic from the flag definitions rather than assuming a NaN test; the wrong first guess cost this lane one probe cycle.

How to reproduce it

Run any checker driver copy from a folder containing a file named results.json and observe it replaced after the run. For the float gate, compare the taken side across positive zero, negative zero, nonzero values, and NaN inputs against a plain equality comparison.

What was confusing or went wrong

Time perception without the clock: the lane estimated forty minutes more had passed than the machine showed, nearly stopping an hour early. Two stack-map computations mixed decimal and hexadecimal offsets and were corrected from snapshot diffs. One diagnostics script initially ignored a register-skip setting and reported phantom differences until fixed.

entry.title: A wrong rewrite passed, and the checker could not see it
entry.summary: A production lane proving small input-system functions found that the checker's comparison of changed global variables ignores where inside a declared range each change happened, so a rewrite that stores the right values at the wrong addresses still passes. Every contract in the lane was rewritten to declare globals one word at a time, which restores the check, and nothing in the checker itself was changed.
entry.content:
A production lane proving small input-system functions found that the checker's comparison of changed global variables ignores where inside a declared range each change happened, so a rewrite that stores the right values at the wrong addresses still passes. Every contract in the lane was rewritten to declare globals one word at a time, which restores the check, and nothing in the checker itself was changed.

What was asked

Rewrite forty small neighbouring functions in Rust and prove each one behaves identically to the original, with a deliberately wrong version per function to show the proof can tell right from wrong.

What was found

Verified Thirty-nine of the forty functions were proved, each over one thousand trials with its wrong version caught. The remaining one cannot be proved as a single contract for a documented checker limitation.

Verified One wrong version stored its result one table slot too low and passed. Reading the checker's comparison code showed why: changed heap and stack words are recorded with their exact offsets, but changed globals are recorded with only the start address of the declared range, so all values written anywhere inside one range compare as an unordered pile. A second experiment confirmed the check runs but is blind to position: a wrong constant at the right place failed, a right value at the wrong place passed.

Verified Declaring each global word as its own range fixes the proofs without touching the checker: the same slot-shifted wrong version then fails, naming the two word addresses. All contracts in the lane use this shape.

Verified Two smaller lessons from the same batch. Direct calls into the encrypted first megabyte of the program are intercepted at the call site and verify normally, so that flag alone is not a reason to defer a function. And three functions read a floating-point value from uninitialized caller stack space; under the checker's zero stack fill they deterministically read zero, which is what the rewrites store, with the limitation recorded on each proof.

What was decided or recommended

  • Keep declaring globals one word per range in new contracts until the comparison records word offsets.
  • Consider re-running earlier proofs whose contracts declare multi-word globals ranges with two or more written words: those proofs cannot show which word got which value, and a slot-shifted wrong version is the test that tells.
  • Do not defer functions only because they call into the encrypted region; defer only what the checker cannot intercept.

How to reproduce it

Write a contract whose function stores two different values to two words of one declared globals range, with a wrong version that swaps the two stores. The wrong version passes. Split the range into one range per word and run again: the wrong version fails. The lane's report names the comparison routine and the contracts that demonstrate both outcomes.

What was confusing or went wrong

The passing wrong version first looked like a mistake in the new contract, and only a second, louder wrong version showed the contract was fine and the comparison was weak. Six other first attempts failed for a sillier reason: the lane wrote callee arguments in push order instead of call order, which the checker caught every time.

entry.title: Same-period contract cyclers can starve whole code regions
entry.summary: Verified A production lane verifying a large ped-task function found that three groups of check trials never ran, not because the paths were rare but because the contract's cycling value lists all shared one period and stayed phase-locked: the trials that reached a region never carried the values that region needed. Giving the cyclers coprime periods fixed it, and all fifty helper stand-ins then fired.
entry.content:
Verified A production lane verifying a large ped-task function found that three groups of check trials never ran, not because the paths were rare but because the contract's cycling value lists all shared one period and stayed phase-locked: the trials that reached a region never carried the values that region needed. Giving the cyclers coprime periods fixed it, and all fifty helper stand-ins then fired.

What was asked

Rewrite one large game function in Rust and prove it identical with the checker, covering every helper it calls.

What was found

Verified Per-trial cycling lists (helper answers, pinned heap words) advance in lock-step by trial number. Three locks were found by reading per-helper fire counts:

  • One helper shared a single answer list between its gate call and its loop calls, so the loop-exhaustion path and the poll-fail path could never co-occur. Splitting the two call sites across two helper entries with independent lists fixed it.
  • Three period-four cyclers (a bypass-flag pin, an aux pin, a null-or-pointer answer list) all put their active value on the same trials, so the bypass always skipped the aux path. Moving one pin's active slot fixed it.
  • Several period-two and period-three answer lists aligned with the conditions that reach them, hiding branches. Coprime periods (four, five, eight) made every combination occur.

Verified Two smaller traps in the same function: float answers delivered in a vector register must be read as plain 32-bit words (a float-typed read picks up unrelated floating-point-stack leftovers), and the original's frame keeps two words of floating-point control-word residue that later snapshots observe, so the rewrite seeds them.

What was decided or recommended

When two cycling lists must combine (a reach condition plus a branch value), give them different periods so the combination occurs by arithmetic rather than luck, and check per-helper fire counts before the full run. A helper with zero firings after hundreds of trials is a lock, not bad luck.

How to reproduce it

Run any multi-branch contract, read the per-helper fire counts in the verdict, and list which trial residues reach each region versus which residues each cycler needs. The lane's generator script and contract show the fixed periods.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first full run passed every trial yet stayed vacuous with three helpers unfired, which looked like rarity until the residues were written out. A later period change silently re-locked two other regions the same way, found the same way. Nothing about the failure pointed at periods; only the fire counts did.
